extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and critics of poetry, drama, and classical literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic and dramatic works (especially tragedy), laying out the distinguishing features of poetic arts, the formal definition of tragedy, and the six constituent parts of tragedy with their relative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts employ different media of imitation: 'in the music of the flute and of the lyre, “harmony” and rhythm alone are employed; also in other arts, such as that of the shepherd’s pipe, which are essentially similar to these. In dancing, rhythm alone is used without “harmony”; ... There is another art which imitates by means of language alone, and that either in prose or verse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate medium(s) for the art: music may use harmony and rhythm; dance uses rhythm alone; language-based arts may use prose or verse. Some poetic forms combine all three (rhythm, tune, metre) — e.g., dithyrambic and nomic poetry, and also tragedy and comedy in certain respects. Choose and coordinate medium(s) to suit the imitation being attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (types of persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action, whom we represent as either better than in real life, worse than in real life, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to portray characters elevated (Homer), true-to-life (Cleophon), or degraded/worse (Hegemon, Nicochares). This choice shapes the work's moral tone and genre (e.g., tragedy tends to represent men better, comedy worse). Painting analogies (Polygnotus vs Pauson vs Dionysius) illustrate corresponding approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs dramatic presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the same medium and objects the poet may imitate by narration (taking another personality as Homer does, or speaking in his own person) or he may present all his characters as living and moving before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between narrative mode and dramatic enactment: narration reports action, while dramatic presentation stages it directly. This choice affects immediacy, audience experience, and which poetic devices are most appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy must present a serious, whole action (not a mere episode) of sufficient scope (magnitude). Language should be ornamented (rhythm, harmony, song) and the action shown rather than merely told. The intended emotional effect (pity and fear leading to catharsis/purgation) is part of the definition and a success criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts that determine a tragedy’s quality are Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy as the evaluation checklist: two parts constitute the medium of imitation (Diction and Song), one the manner, and three the objects of imitation. Every play should be inspected for each part, and the interplay among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the imitation of the action — by plot I mean the arrangement of the incidents. The Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so they form a coherent, causally linked whole leading to an end; prioritize unity and an artistically-constructed sequence. A well-constructed plot (including peripeteia/reversal and anagnorisis/recognition) produces the essential tragic effects even if diction or character are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and unity of action (temporal unity & completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun, or but slightly to exceed this limit; action should be serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for unity and completeness: a single, coherent action with a clear beginning, middle and end. Time-limits (unity of time) are recommended for concentrated dramatic effect; episodic or sprawling actions resemble Epic and alter the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Character
rubrics_metrics.description: By Character I mean that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents. Character reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters through choices and actions that reveal moral aims. Character is subsidiary to plot (it serves the action) and ranks second in importance. Speeches that fail to show choice or avoidance are not expressive of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (intellectual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; it is found where something is proved to be or not to be, or a general maxim is enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought covers the arguments, reasoning, and the capacity to enunciate general truths or proofs within the play — akin to rhetorical function. Ensure speeches and moments of reasoning are pertinent and contribute to the dramatic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (expression in words and metrical arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same both in verse and prose. By diction I mean the mere metrical arrangement of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word choice and metrical form appropriate to the dialogue and genre. The iambic is particularly suited to colloquial dialogue; diction should serve clarity of meaning and fit the dramatic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the remaining elements Song holds the chief place among the embellishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use song (choral lyric, sung passages) as a principal ornament where appropriate; some parts of a tragedy are rendered with the aid of song, and it contributes strongly to the work’s emotional and aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (staging and visual effects) as least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectacle has, indeed, an emotional attraction of its own, but, of all the parts, it is the least artistic, and connected least with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat spectacle as subsidiary: it can heighten emotion but is not the poet’s principal art. The poet’s power should be evident even apart from staging, actors, and visual effects; do not rely on spectacle to carry weak plot or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and Recognition as plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The most powerful elements of emotional interest in Tragedy — Peripeteia or Reversal of Intention, and Recognition scenes — are parts of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reversals and recognitions to arise naturally from the causal network of incidents; these moments are central to producing pity and fear and thereby catharsis. Avoid contrived or unmotivated reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s object and the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of characters of a lower type — not, however, in the full sense of the word bad, the Ludicrous being merely a subdivision of the 'ugly.' It consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing comic works, aim to portray defects or absurdities that provoke laughter without real harm. Comedy typically represents men as worse than they are and differs historically and formally from tragedy; its devices include masks and lampooning measures (iambic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy distinctions (form, metre, and temporality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry agrees with Tragedy in so far as it is a narration in verse of characters of a higher type. They differ in that Epic poetry admits but one kind of metre, and is narrative in form; Epic action has no limits of time, whereas Tragedy tends to confine itself to a single day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genre by formal choices: use sustained hexameter narrative for Epic (broad temporal scope) and dramatic, mixed measures and enacted scenes with temporal unity for Tragedy. Know which constituent elements are shared and which are peculiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and psychological basis of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry sprang from (1) the instinct of imitation implanted in man from childhood, and (2) the instinct for 'harmony' and rhythm; men take pleasure in imitation and in learning that imitation affords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize imitation and rhythmic/harmonic pleasure as drivers of poetic effect: realism, faithful execution, learning-by-looking, and metrical shaping can be harnessed deliberately to engage audiences. Use imitation and rhythmic devices to amplify learning and pleasure.
